title: Trump Threatens to Bomb Oman Over Hormuz Traffic Deal as Ceasefire Window Closes; IAEA Finds Tons of Nuclear Material in Syria
subhead: The two-month US-Iran negotiation window expired with no deal, Brent pushed above $90, and Trump escalated against a longtime Gulf partner over its plan to manage Hormuz shipping with Tehran. Separately, the IAEA disclosed tons of undeclared nuclear material in Syria.

sections.heading: Trump Threatens Oman as Hormuz Deal With Iran Takes Shape
sections.body:
US President Donald Trump threatened to bomb Oman because Washington is unhappy with a deal Muscat is close to signing with Iran to manage ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, two regional officials told Reuters on Tuesday. The administration objects to joint Iranian-Omani management of the strait's exit route and to Oman collecting voluntary fees from vessels, even for security and environmental purposes. It was the second time Trump has threatened Oman — in May he said it would 'behave just like everybody else, or we will have to blow them up.' On Monday he told Fox News, 'If Oman gets in the way, we'll bomb the shit out of them,' and posted a map on social media depicting the strait as US territory.

Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi responded on X that Trump's 'delusion regarding the Strait of Hormuz will soon either be corrected, or we will correct this deluded man's delusions for him.' The White House declined to comment beyond Trump's Oval Office remarks that he 'likes the idea of declaring it a territory.'
sections.whyItMatters: Oman is the one Gulf state that has kept a working channel to Tehran and was positioning itself as the mediator to reopen the strait. Trump's threat to bomb a US strategic partner over a traffic-management fee scheme signals Washington is willing to burn its last diplomatic bridge in the Gulf — and that the reopening of Hormuz now hinges on a US-Iran standoff with no neutral broker left.

sections.heading: Ceasefire Window Expires, Brent Tops $90 as Market Prices a Long Closure
sections.body:
The two-month window to negotiate a peace deal in the US-Iran war expired on Monday with no breakthrough. Brent crude rose above $90 a barrel for the first time since 30 July, trading at $91.63 on Tuesday morning, according to the Guardian. Trump demanded Tehran 'put up the white flag of surrender' in a Fox News interview, while an Iranian official told Reuters Tehran would shift to a 'fully offensive' military stance. A cargo ship was attacked transiting the strait early Tuesday, per the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency, and Iran's military spokesperson Ebrahim Zolfaghari said vessels attempting to pass would 'find several beautiful holes in their hulls.'

Ship-tracking firm Kpler counted just six commodity ships transiting the waterway on Monday, up slightly from five over the whole weekend. Deutsche Bank analysts wrote that rising prices reflect investors pricing in 'a more extended closure' of the strait, and IG analyst Angeline Ong said Trump's Oman threat could be 'the moment the oil market shifts from pricing a temporary disruption to pricing a prolonged one.'
sections.whyItMatters: The market is no longer treating Hormuz as a reversible shock. With roughly a quarter of global seaborne oil normally transiting the strait and transit volumes near zero, the question has shifted from when the strait reopens to what a prolonged closure does to global inventories, refining margins and inflation into the winter.

sections.heading: Saudi Aramco Resumes Loadings From Inside the Strait
sections.body:
Saudi Aramco resumed oil loading from inside the Strait of Hormuz last week and has more tankers waiting to load, as the state energy giant offers spot heavy crude cargoes, according to shipping data and trade sources cited by Reuters. The resumption comes even as Iran insists the waterway remains shut and as the US and Iran trade sharply different accounts of its status.

The move is notable because Saudi Arabia's main export terminals at Ras Tanura and Juaymah sit on the Gulf side of the strait, meaning loadings there depend on the passage being navigable. Aramco's willingness to offer spot cargoes suggests at least partial confidence in moving vessels through, or a bet that the US-backed push to reopen the strait will hold.
sections.whyItMatters: Saudi Arabia is the Gulf producer with the most to lose from a closed strait, and its decision to resume loadings is a concrete signal — separate from Washington's rhetoric — that at least some commercial traffic is moving again. It also puts Saudi commercial interests in direct tension with Iran's stated position that the strait stays shut until US conditions are met.

sections.heading: EU Gas Stocks at 5-Year Low; Pakistan Pays Record Spot LNG Prices
sections.body:
European Union gas storage levels have dropped to their lowest mid-August level in five years as Middle East LNG disruption persists, Daily Sabah reported, with analysts expecting the bloc to face a tight winter. The strain is hitting importers hardest. Pakistan's power generation costs jumped 38% in July year-on-year as the country paid the highest spot LNG prices in four years, according to brokerage Arif Habib Limited, after cargoes from its long-term term supplier Qatar were stranded by the renewed closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

State-controlled importer Pakistan LNG Limited has issued several tenders for July and August delivery and is willing to pay top dollar to secure supply, per OilPrice.com. The pattern — a South Asian importer forced onto the spot market at four-year-high prices because a Gulf term supplier cannot deliver — is being repeated across Asia as the strait closure ripples through LNG and crude supply chains.
sections.whyItMatters: The Hormuz closure is no longer just an oil story. It is hitting gas storage in Europe and forcing price-sensitive importers like Pakistan to absorb record spot costs, which will feed into electricity tariffs and fiscal strain. The longer the strait stays closed, the more these costs compound into winter supply risk for both Europe and South Asia.

sections.heading: IAEA Finds Tons of Undeclared Nuclear Material in Syria
sections.body:
IAEA chief Rafael Grossi said Tuesday that inspectors found 'tons of nuclear materials that could be put to bad use' at a previously undisclosed site in Syria, dating from the era of the ousted Assad government. Grossi, speaking at a press conference in Damascus with Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani, said the material would be 'accounted for' and placed within international safeguards. Syria declared the site voluntarily in a letter to the agency on July 17, and al-Shaibani said the material was not dangerous and would remain in Syrian custody, subject to IAEA guarantees, with Syria retaining the right to use it for civil and peaceful purposes.

Grossi also visited a site in Deir Ezzor in eastern Syria, according to the Telegraph. The disclosure comes as the IAEA works to secure nuclear material left over from the Assad era, and as the US-Iran war has put regional nuclear questions back at the center of attention.
sections.whyItMatters: The discovery of tons of undeclared nuclear material in post-Assad Syria is a reminder that the region's nuclear legacy extends beyond Iran. It tests whether the new Syrian government will cooperate with the IAEA on safeguards, and it adds a fresh nuclear-security dimension to an already volatile Middle East energy and security landscape.

sections.heading: Oman Oil Spill Salvage Hampered by Weather
sections.body:
Salvage and clean-up efforts for the grounded tanker Caroline Bezengi, which has been leaking Russian crude in a protected marine area off Oman's coast, are being hampered by weather and technical challenges, Oman's state news agency reported Monday, per Reuters. The spill, which has spread largely unchecked for weeks, has already reached Oman's coastline and threatens to become one of the world's worst in years, according to the UN agency and Oman's environment authority.

Risk firm Ambrey is coordinating the salvage operation, with specialist vessels heading to the area. The spill is a direct consequence of the shadow-fleet trade in Russian crude moving through the Gulf amid the war, and it has now become an environmental and diplomatic problem for Oman — the same country Trump is now threatening.
sections.whyItMatters: The Caroline Bezengi spill is the physical cost of the shadow-fleet oil trade colliding with a closed strait. It is also politically awkward for Oman, which is simultaneously trying to mediate the Hormuz reopening while dealing with a Russian-crude environmental disaster on its own coast — and now facing US threats over its Iran diplomacy.

bottomLine: The US-Iran negotiation window closed with no deal, Brent pushed above $90, and Trump escalated against Oman — the one Gulf state still talking to Tehran — over its plan to manage Hormuz traffic, effectively removing the last neutral broker from the equation. The market is now pricing a prolonged closure rather than a temporary shock, with EU gas stocks at a five-year low and Pakistan absorbing record spot LNG costs. Separately, the IAEA's disclosure of tons of undeclared nuclear material in Syria adds a new nuclear-security layer to a region already defined by the Hormuz standoff. The near-term question is whether any diplomatic path to reopening the strait survives Trump's threats to the Gulf's would-be mediators.
sources: Reuters, The Guardian, AsiaOne, Daily Sabah, OilPrice.com, Arif Habib Limited, The Telegraph, Yahoo News, Al Arabiya, Kpler, Deutsche Bank, IG
